Security

Clusters runs on Supabase (database and sign-in, in AWS us-west-2) and Cloudflare (website, API, files and live editing), and both encrypt stored data. Every connection is HTTPS. Sign-in is an emailed code or a passkey, with no password to leak. A cluster is seen only by its workspace and people you share it with, and the database enforces access on every table. API keys and connected-app tokens are stored only as hashes, and an AI app can delete only if you allow it. Report a vulnerability to security@soleilpictures.com.

Updated November 5, 2026

Clusters keeps film and creative work: scripts, references, cuts in progress. This page says how that work is protected, in plain words, and only what is true today. Where a protection belongs to one of our providers, it says so and links to theirs.

Report a vulnerability

Email security@soleilpictures.com. Please include:

  • what you found, and where (a page, an API route, an MCP tool)
  • the steps to reproduce it
  • what someone could do with it

A few ground rules while you look:

  • Use your own account and your own test data. Don't open, change or delete anyone else's.
  • Don't run tests that slow the service down for others, and don't send spam or invitations to people who didn't ask for them.
  • Give us a fair chance to fix it before you tell anyone else.

We read every report and reply from the same address. There is no paid bug bounty, but we're glad to credit you when the fix ships, if you'd like. Our security.txt has the same contact.

Where your data lives

Clusters is run from the United States. Each part runs on one provider:

WhatProvider
Your account, clusters, cards, documents, comments and messagesSupabase (Postgres database and sign-in), in AWS us-west-2, Oregon
Uploaded files, and their backup copyCloudflare R2. Some message attachments and a few older card pictures are in Supabase storage
The website, the API and the MCP serverCloudflare Workers
Live editing: who's here, and changes as they happenCloudflare Durable Objects
Picture descriptions for search and tagsCloudflare Workers AI, which doesn't keep the picture or train on it
PaymentsStripe. Card details are typed on Stripe's page and never reach Clusters
EmailResend
Making videos and audio play in every browser, previews of photos and documents browsers can't open, and ScoutFly.io

The full list, including the Meta measurement used on public pages, is in the Privacy Policy.

Encryption

  • On the way. Every connection uses HTTPS. A plain http address is sent to HTTPS, and browsers are told to use only HTTPS for this site and every address under it.
  • At rest. Stored data is encrypted by the provider that holds it: Supabase encrypts the database with AES-256 (Supabase security), Cloudflare R2 encrypts files with AES-256 (R2 data security), and Durable Objects are encrypted at rest (Durable Objects data security). Stripe encrypts card numbers with AES-256 and is certified PCI Service Provider Level 1 (Stripe security).
  • Keys and tokens. API keys and connected-app tokens are kept only as a one-way hash. A key is shown once, when you make it, and can't be read back, even by us.

Signing in

  • An emailed code or a passkey. Your account has no password to set, reuse or leak. (The one exception is an internal demo account that app directories use to review Clusters.)
  • Passkeys. Only a public key reaches us; the passkey itself stays with your device or its password manager, and using it usually asks for your face, fingerprint or device PIN. You can see and remove your passkeys in Settings › Profile, and a removed one stops working at once.
  • Your inbox is the proof. Joining a team, accepting an invitation by address or joining by company domain needs a session that started from that inbox (a code or link we emailed), or from a passkey saved while signed in that way.
  • New accounts wait. For its first 72 hours an account can't make API keys or add webhooks, and can connect only the main AI assistants and apps that sign in through your own computer, as coding tools do. This slows down throwaway accounts.
  • Signing out signs you out on every device. A page already open on another device can keep working for a short while, until its current sign-in expires. An account banned for abuse is signed out everywhere, and its links, invitations and keys stop working.

Who can see what

  • Your workspace, your people. A cluster is visible to the people in its workspace and to anyone you share it with. A workspace of your own is just you until you invite someone or make a link. On a Team, team workspaces are open to the team.
  • Roles. A workspace has an owner, co-owners, editors and viewers. Viewers can open, comment and vote but never change anything. Only the owner can delete a workspace or hand it over.
  • Links. A public link is always view-only, asks search engines not to list it unless you turn that on, can be set to expire, and can be turned off at any time. An edit link grants nothing by itself: the person has to sign in and press Join. See Sharing.
  • When someone leaves or is removed, the links and invitations they made end, the files they shared stop reaching people, they leave the workspace's conversations, and the webhooks and service accounts they set up are turned off.
  • The database enforces it. Every table has row-level security, so who can read or change a row is checked by the database itself, the same way for the app, the API and connected apps. An automatic check runs every day and alerts us if any table has that protection turned off, or a new rule lets anyone add rows.

On a Team

  • The owner and admins manage people, seats and how people join. Only the owner changes the card or closes the team.
  • The owner and admins can open every team workspace, including private ones, and only they see members' email addresses.
  • Joining by company email domain needs the domain proved with a DNS record, and free email providers can't be used for it.

See Team.

API, MCP and connected apps

  • A key acts as you. It reaches exactly what your account reaches, under the same database rules as the app. A key made in Settings › Connections starts read-only unless you choose more, and revoking it works at once.
  • Separate permissions. Access comes in parts (delete · read · write), and deleting is its own permission, never part of write.
  • Connected apps (OAuth), such as Claude or ChatGPT through MCP. You approve each one in your browser, on a screen that lists what it may do. An app that asks to read and write can't delete unless you also tick Allow deleting, and one that asks to delete says so there first. Sign-in uses PKCE. An access token lasts 60 minutes. Each renewal token works once (a retry within 30 seconds is allowed), and one reused after that ends the connection. After 180 days an app has to be approved again. Disconnecting an app works at once.
  • The MCP server holds no keys of its own. Every call it makes is yours, held to the permission that call needs. Text people wrote is marked as data for the assistant, so instructions hidden in a card aren't treated as commands.
  • Limits. A personal key can make 1000 requests an hour.
  • A record of changes. Writes made through the API or MCP are logged with the key or app that made them, and you can read that log through the API. Records are deleted after 30 days.
  • Webhooks are signed with HMAC-SHA256 using a secret for that webhook, go only to public HTTPS addresses, never follow redirects, and can be set up only by the workspace owner.

See Authentication and OAuth.

Backups and deleting your data

  • The database is backed up every night. The backup is encrypted before it leaves the backup job, stored apart from the live database, and then read back to check it arrived whole. The database provider keeps its own backups as well.
  • Files uploaded to clusters are copied by an hourly job to a separate backup store. Message attachments kept in Supabase storage aren't part of that copy.
  • Deleted clusters stay in Trash for 30 days, then are deleted for good.
  • Deleting your account in Settings › Profile takes effect at once and can't be undone. A file's backup copy isn't removed when you delete it yet, and the database provider's backups can hold deleted information until they are replaced. The Privacy Policy has the details, and Data and privacy says how to get everything out first.

How the code is looked after

  • Automated tests run on every change, including one that fails when these public docs no longer match the code.
  • GitHub scans the code for security problems (CodeQL), raises and opens fixes for vulnerable dependencies (Dependabot), and blocks secrets from being committed (secret scanning with push protection).
  • Text people write is cleaned before it is shown, so it can't run script in someone else's browser. Uploaded files are served so they can't run script on our site.
  • The site can't be framed by another site, and browsers are told not to guess file types.

Certifications

Clusters has no SOC 2, ISO 27001 or similar certification of its own, and has not had a third-party penetration test. The providers it runs on publish theirs: Supabase, Cloudflare and Stripe.

Frequently asked questions

Is Soleil Clusters SOC 2 certified?

No. Clusters has no SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certification of its own and has not had a third-party penetration test. The providers it runs on, Supabase, Cloudflare and Stripe, publish their own certifications. This page says what is in place instead.

How do I report a security problem?

Email security@soleilpictures.com with what you found and how to reproduce it. The same address is in /.well-known/security.txt.

Where is my data stored?

The database and sign-in run on Supabase in AWS us-west-2 (Oregon, United States). Files are stored on Cloudflare, which also runs the website, the API and live editing. Payments are handled by Stripe, and card details are typed on Stripe's own page, never on Clusters.

Can an AI app I connect delete my clusters?

Only if you let it. The approval screen lists what an app may do. An app that asks to read and write can't delete unless you also tick Allow deleting, and an app that asks to delete shows Delete there before you approve. You can disconnect an app at any time and it stops working at once.

Do you offer two-step sign-in or single sign-on (SSO)?

Not today. Sign-in is an emailed one-time code or a passkey, and using a passkey usually asks for your face, fingerprint or device PIN. For single sign-on on a Team, use Talk to us on the pricing page.
